vignette:
Dorothea was seventy-three years old, a forester who had spent forty years reading the quiet language of trees and soil, but she could not read the silence of a room. The trauma that had shaped her was not a single explosion but a long, slow erosion of safety, beginning when she was a child and her mother would lock her in a closet for hours. The memory was not a clear picture but a felt sense—the smell of old coats, the way her own breath sounded too loud, and the absolute certainty that no one was coming. What frightened her most now was not the memory itself but the way it could be summoned by a sound: the click of a door latching, the sudden drop of noise when a radio was turned off. She had come to believe that her life had been destroyed by those years, that the person she might have been was buried somewhere in that dark, and that you could never know who would harm you, because the person who was supposed to protect you had been the one to shut the door.

Dorothea worked alone, which suited her. She could spend eight hours walking a tract of land without hearing another human voice. But her job required occasional meetings with landowners, and those were almost always women. Being alone with a woman, even a friendly one, made her chest tighten. She would feel her skin go cold, her mind racing with the sense that she was being watched, judged, that at any moment the woman’s face would change. She had learned to schedule these meetings outdoors, on the move, so that there was always a path to walk away. But the problem was worse in the office. The silence of a closed room, the way a conversation could pause and leave nothing but the hum of fluorescent lights—that was the worst. It felt like being lowered into a well.

To manage the dread, Dorothea had developed habits that she knew were not healthy but that she could not stop. She avoided exercise, because the sound of her own breathing, heavy and rhythmic in a quiet space, reminded her of trying not to cry in the closet. She avoided being alone in her house, so she kept the television on constantly, even when she was not watching it. And she spent money impulsively—online orders for tools she did not need, books she would never read—because the act of clicking “buy” gave her a brief, chemical relief from the feeling that she was not a person, just an object that had been put away and forgotten. She had come to believe that these strategies were the only things keeping her from falling apart, but in the quiet moments after a purchase, the shame would arrive, and with it the old conviction that her life had been destroyed, that she was beyond repair.

The cycle was tightening. The more she spent, the more she felt like a failure, and the more she needed to spend again to escape that feeling. The more she avoided silence, the more sensitive she became to it; a sudden quiet in the grocery store could make her heart pound so hard she had to leave her cart and walk out. She had begun to dread the evenings, when the forest work was done and she had to return to her small house, where the only sound was the refrigerator and her own footsteps. She had stopped answering the phone. She had stopped calling her daughter, because the silence on the other end of the line, even for a second, felt like a trap door opening.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in the forest. She had been marking a boundary line when she heard nothing—no birds, no wind—and she froze, unable to move, convinced that someone was standing behind her. She turned around and there was no one, but she could not shake the feeling. She sat down on a log and cried for the first time in years. She was afraid that she was losing her mind, but more than that, she was afraid of spending the rest of her life in that closet, even though she had walked out of it sixty-five years ago. She wanted to know if it was possible to feel like a person again, or if that part of her was truly gone.
